did_you_know.text: The word *asham* refers to an offering connected with guilt and making amends, not merely punishment. It is called “most holy,” a particularly high level of sacredness.
The guilt offering was slaughtered in the same place as the burnt offering. This suggests that each type of offering did not have its own separate slaughtering area.
*Alyah* is the fatty tail found especially on fat-tailed sheep. In the ancient world, this kind of fat was considered a prized part of the offering.
The guilt offering could be eaten only by male priests and within the sacred area. Thus, eating the offering was itself part of the Temple service.
This verse compares the sin offering and the guilt offering, saying that they follow “one law.” In both cases, the priest who performs the atonement receives the edible meat.
The three baking utensils mentioned here represent different cooking methods: an oven, a deep pan, and a flat griddle. Even the way the grain offering was prepared was regulated.
Unlike offerings that were baked or cooked, a grain offering mixed with oil or left dry was divided equally among Aaron’s sons. The phrase “each like his brother” emphasizes this principle.
A thanksgiving offering included several kinds of bread: loaves, wafers, and cakes made from fine flour. The variety of preparations made it a substantial thanksgiving meal.
Alongside the unleavened breads of the thanksgiving offering, leavened bread was also brought. This shows that the prohibition of leaven did not apply identically to every offering.
The meat of the thanksgiving offering had to be eaten on the day it was brought. This fits its character as a shared meal of gratitude rather than food kept for a long time.
A vow or freewill offering could be eaten on the following day as well. In this respect, it differed from the thanksgiving offering, which had to be eaten within one day.
The ban on eating blood is stated to apply “in all your settlements,” not only during Temple worship. It is therefore presented as a dietary rule binding the Israelites wherever they lived.
The chapter ends by naming six types of offerings: burnt, grain, sin, guilt, ordination, and well-being offerings. The list summarizes the system discussed in the opening chapters of Leviticus.
